rv.q: 'That Championship Season' has been revived to excellent effect by a talented, committed ensemble of actors.

Despite its creation in a tumultuous era, this never was a more than a solid piece of middlebrow message-naturalism. And despite the care and affection lavished on the handsome production, it remains a male-bonding parlor drama that signals its big secrets more clearly than it justifies a high-profile revival.
That Championship Season, a shocker in 1972, is a season or 40 out of date, its fire-bell-in-the-night philippics now playing as crude Tourettic barks.

That the friend is played by Frances McDormand - giving perhaps the most satisfying stage performance of her career - intensifies by magnitudes the electric unease, the uncomfortable feeling that the binding of a "perfect" life tenuously held together is about to come undone.
Mr. Miller's play... looks less like a penetrating study... than a cartoon drawn with an extra-thick Magic Marker.
But the stars are just as stymied as the rest of the ensemble by the play’s schematic structure and transparent characters.
But Gregory Mosher’s star-studded production — the cast also includes Kiefer Sutherland, Chris Noth and Jim Gaffigan — is a train wreck.
That Championship Season is an enjoyable, though somewhat outdated look at a time when leaders, like Nixon and Lombardi, were still blindly obeyed.
The arguments and diatribes fueling the play seldom encourage reflection, and like real-life drunken banter, can grow tedious.
As a museum piece the production succeeds. But if the producers were aiming higher, I'd have to say they dropped the ball.
Regarded as individual human beings, they don't make much sense.
Unfortunately, what emerges is a thinly written, awkwardly constructed melodrama.

But as currently revived on Broadway for the first time — with an all-star cast including Kiefer Sutherland, Chris Noth, Jason Patric (the playwright's son), Brian Cox and Jim Gaffigan — the only thing you'll find shocking is how terribly the play has aged.
Unfortunately for now, it's a former winner that should have stayed in retirement.
But, one can’t escape the feeling that there is still something missing here.
